senses.gloss:
Nighaṇṭu
(‘that which explains the words,’ ‘dictionary’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu religious tradition declares that all words—including the words of our daily life and usage—have been derived from the वेदस्. As the volume of the वेदस् grew through new revelations, there arose the need for proper and correct understanding of the words and phrases by which the Vedic rituals could be performed properly. Then alone, the results predicated could be attained.
This need led to the compilation of the Nighaṇṭu or the first Vedic Lexicon. This work commands the same respect as towards the वेदस् themselves. The compiler is not known.
Yāska’s commentary on it (800 B.C.)—known as the Nirukta—is available even now. Another known as Nighaṇṭu-nirvacana by Devarāja Yajvan (12th cent. A. D.) is also available. This work purports to supply additional material on the Nighaṇṭu.
The Nighaṇṭu has five adhyāyas or chapters. The first three are known as the Naighaṇṭuka Kāṇḍa, the fourth as the Naigama Kāṇḍa and the last as the Daivata Kāṇḍa.
The Naighaṇṭuka Kāṇḍa deals with synonyms, the total numbers of words being 1341.
The Naigama Kāṇḍa deals with homonyms (ekapadi) whose number comes to 278.
The Daivata Kāṇḍa deals with the names of deities in the three regions: earth, sky and हेअवेन्. They total up to 151.
This takes the grand total of the words of the Nighaṇṭu to 1770.
The topics include: physical elements like the earth, water and air; objects of nature like clouds, dawn, day and night; the human body and its limbs; objects and qualities associated with people, such as prosperity, anger and fighting; physical abstract qualities like lightness and heaviness.
If the word ‘nighaṇṭu’ is understood in a more general way as a ‘dictionary,’ the following Sanskrit-Sanskrit dictionaries may be mentioned:
Amarakośa of अमरसिṁह, also called Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (A. D. 500).
Anekārthasamuccaya of Śāśvata (6th cent. A. D.).
Anekārthadhvanimañjarī of Mahākṣapaṇaka (A. D. 900).
Vaijayantīkośa of यादवप्रकाश. (A. D. 1100).
Abhidhānaratnamālā of हलायुध (A. D. 950) more popularly known as the Halāyudhakośa.
Nānārthaśabdakośa (Medinīkośa) by Medinīkara (A. D. 1100).
Nighaṇṭus or dictionaries dealing with special topics like botany and medicine were also composed in later times.
